name: African Blue Lily

symptoms.name: Vomiting
symptoms.notes: Saponins throughout the plant irritate the gastrointestinal mucosa, commonly causing vomiting.

symptoms.name: Excess salivation
symptoms.notes: Drooling (hypersalivation) occurs as part of the saponin-driven gastrointestinal irritation and nausea.

symptoms.name: Diarrhea
symptoms.notes: Saponins irritate the GI tract, causing diarrhea. Unlike true lilies, it does not cause acute renal failure.

chemicals.name: Saponins
chemicals.description: Saponins irritate the gastrointestinal mucosa. Ingestion typically causes mild signs such as vomiting, excessive salivation (drooling), and diarrhea. African Blue Lily is not a true lily (Lilium species) and does not cause the acute kidney failure associated with true lilies.
chemicals.concentration_notes: Saponins are found throughout the plant. Toxicity is generally minimal unless larger amounts are ingested.

treatments.name: Oral Rinsing
treatments.description: Remove any remaining plant material from the mouth and rinse or wipe the oral cavity with water.
treatments.notes: Clearing residual plant material helps reduce ongoing exposure to the saponins that irritate the gastrointestinal and oral mucosa.

treatments.name: Symptomatic Supportive Care
treatments.description: Administration of medications to manage specific symptoms, such as vomiting or diarrhea.
treatments.notes: Since the plant acts as a gastrointestinal irritant causing vomiting, drooling, and diarrhea, care is symptomatic, targeting these signs as they resolve. Unlike true lilies, aggressive fluid therapy for kidney failure is not required for Agapanthus unless dehydration occurs.

safetyNotes: Symptoms: Vomiting, diarrhea, and excessive drooling are the most common signs of ingestion.
Not a true lily: Unlike Lilium or Hemerocallis species, this plant does not cause kidney failure, making it significantly less dangerous — but it is still not safe to ingest.
Action: Monitor your cat after any suspected ingestion; contact a vet if symptoms persist or worsen.
description: African Blue Lily (Agapanthus) is often mistaken for a true lily, but it belongs to a different plant family and does not cause the acute kidney failure associated with true lilies (Lilium and Hemerocallis species). However, it is mildly toxic to cats: saponins found throughout the plant can cause gastrointestinal distress (vomiting, drooling, diarrhea) when any part — including the leaves, stems, or roots — is ingested. Cats are sometimes attracted to its grass-like foliage, so households with this plant should monitor access.
